statements.quote:
We present an interactive demo of our project at https://joongishin.github.io/
problemReframing_llm/

This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution
International 4.0 License.

By inferring key information (e.g., why the problem
is difficult to solve and who the potential stakeholders are) from a
problem description, the structured approach could help design-
ers spot alternative perspectives on the initial problem (Appendix
A.2 details the steps for this).
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.3, pointer to the structured-approach materials

statements.quote:
In the end, we had 280 participants (145
identifying as women, 128 as men, and seven as “other”; other
demographics are presented in Appendix E), as shown in Figure 8.
statements.locator: p. 6, Section 4.2, pointer to Appendix E

statements.quote:
These
problems (described in Appendix C) are widely relatable and can
be understood without the benefit of domain-specific knowledge.
Via a pilot study (N = 36), we confirmed that the problems had an
appropriate level of difficulty by examining participants’ creation of
a variety of low- and high-quality frames (see Appendix D). Table
1 presents one of the problems and some frames created for it.

We designed prompts and interfaces to imple-
ment the direct and structured approaches (see Appendix A).

For this purpose, we designed a quiz with five multiple-choice ques-
tions based on the key concept, activity, and outcome of problem
reframing [15, 19, 65] where each question had four response op-
tions, among which were 1–2 correct answers (see Appendix B).

The
example problem frames and their qualities are shown in Table 1.

The distribution plot on the left shows how many questions about problem reframing the participants answered
correctly (see Appendix B for correct answers).

Accordingly, we set up a system role that describes problem reframing and upcoming tasks (see Table 3), then tested
our prompts by using the model that performed best at the time of the research (GPT-4o).
statements.locator: p. 17, Appendix A, system prompt in Table 3

statements.quote: Below, we introduce the prompts and system design of the direct and the structured approach.
statements.locator: p. 17, Appendix A, concluding sentence of the introduction

statements.quote:
In
this interface, presented in Figure 12, users read a problem description, press the button to (re)generate alternative problem frames, and build
on the LLM-generated frames. To make the process iterative, we designed two prompts each comprising input, task, and output components
(shown in Table 4).
statements.locator: p. 17, Appendix A.1, interface and direct-approach prompts

statements.quote:
We implemented an interface wherein LLM-generated contents are shown in each
window, grouped by similarity of purpose in problem reframing (see Figure 14). In a similarity to the direct approach, users can click the
“Reframe” button to prompt the LLMs to go through the entire set of steps or use a refresh button offered in each content window to prompt
the LLMs to generate local content. We designed step-specific prompts for this as shown in tables 5, 6, 7, and 8. Overall, we designed these
to enable a prompt-chaining technique [84], whereby the outputs can be taken as input to the next prompt. Our design decisions on the
prompts are shown in the corresponding tables.
statements.locator: p. 19, Appendix A.2, interface and structured-approach prompts

statements.quote: We designed a quiz to test participants’ competence in problem reframing. This is reproduced as Table 9.
We articulated three design problems for reframing, described below.
statements.locator: p. 24, Appendix C, opening sentence; problems continue on p. 25

statements.quote: We conducted a pilot study to confirm the feasibility of reframing the design problems we had prepared (reproduced in Appendix C).

Its nine pages match the extracted text of the saved PDF's pp. 17-25 exactly, with no embedded files or external links. It supplies prompts, interface descriptions, the quiz, design problems, the pilot description, and aggregate demographics. S1 and S2 coverage refers to these materials, not to participant data. The three boolean fields refer to usable individual-level data, not illustrative quotations or arm descriptions in the paper. No repository-wide license file or license statement was found; the paper itself states CC BY 4.0. README's OpenAI API-key requirement concerns running the proposed demo, not access to repository files.

notes: Checked 2026-10-09. Read all 118,429 characters of the saved markdown, including references and Appendices A-E, and checked the quoted material pointers against PDF text. The saved source is arXiv:2503.01631v1, 3 March 2025, 25 pages. Statements reproduce PDF text verbatim, retaining line wraps and line-end hyphenation. No formal data/code availability, preregistration, repository deposit, or data-on-request statement was found; acknowledgments contain funding information only. The form's data_and_code.data_url and code_url are empty. The only study-specific external materials link in the paper is the project page; its GitHub repository and linked appendix are counted as one deposit, avoiding duplicate counts for the website and its files. DataCite's matching arXiv record is the article, not a data deposit; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01631 was opened successfully (HTTP 200) and did not identify a participant-data deposit. All required repository searches were completed; unsuccessful initial Zenodo requests are explicitly retained with null result counts, followed by successful anonymous requests. No public participant-level or participant-linked output data were confirmed for either S1 or S2. Therefore the public materials cannot supply S1 novelty/usefulness arm means, SDs, SEs or effect sizes (open item 1), per-arm assignment/exclusion counts (item 2), per-frame rater counts or rating aggregation (item 3), or pair-specific tests (item 8), nor a participant-level corpus for diversity measures. They do not resolve S2's unspecified pilot tools (item 7). Published analyzed totals and illustrative frames are not a substitute for the missing records. ACM's landing page was blocked by a bot check, so its supplements and the version-of-record comparison (item 9) remain unverified; medium confidence reflects this limit, not evidence that access to a known dataset is restricted. Other main-text footnote links were checked and returned HTTP 200: https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4o (redirected to https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4o), https://huggingface.co/spaces/ArtificialAnalysis/LLM-Performance-Leaderboard, https://www.prolific.com/, https://www.cloudresearch.com/, and https://www.prolific.com/resources/find-filter-favourite-how-to-select-participants-for-ai-tasks. These are model/platform documentation, not deposits for this study. Reference-list articles and author-profile links were not treated as study-data deposits. No login, account creation, access request, or bot-check bypass was attempted; downloads were inspected in memory.
